lesson.title: No Systematic Drift: Why x-bar Targets mu
lesson.summary: The mean of the sampling distribution of x-bar is exactly equal to the population mean mu, which makes the sample mean an unbiased estimator, just as p-hat was for the population proportion.
lesson.body:
Return to the population of four values, 2, 4, 6, and 8, from the previous chapter, with population mean mu = 5, and the sampling distribution of x-bar for samples of size two: values 3, 4, 6, and 7 each with probability 1/6, and the value 5 with probability 2/6. The mean of that sampling distribution is found by multiplying each possible x-bar by its probability and summing: (3)(1/6) + (4)(1/6) + (5)(2/6) + (6)(1/6) + (7)(1/6). That sum equals (3 + 4 + 10 + 6 + 7)/6 = 30/6 = 5.

That result, 5, is exactly equal to mu, the true population mean. As with the sample proportion, this is not a coincidence specific to this example, it is a general fact that holds for simple random sampling from any population: the mean of the sampling distribution of x-bar always equals mu. Statisticians write this as mu of x-bar equals mu.

This links directly back to the idea of an unbiased estimator introduced earlier in this unit. Because the sampling distribution of x-bar is centered exactly on mu, with no tendency to run systematically high or systematically low, x-bar is an unbiased estimator of mu. The intuition behind this fact is straightforward: each individual observation in a sample is, on average, equal to mu, since the sample is drawn randomly from the population. Averaging n such observations together does not shift that average, it only reduces how much it bounces around, which is the subject of the next chapter.

So both statistics developed in this unit, p-hat and x-bar, share this same reassuring property. Neither one is guaranteed to hit its target on any individual sample, in the four-value example not one of the six possible samples produced x-bar = 5 exactly, yet the sampling distribution as a whole is perfectly centered on the parameter. That is precisely what makes both statistics reasonable choices for estimation in the first place.
